title: Why Is New York Dumping Its High School Exit Exam?
author: Neetu Arnold
summary: Neetu Arnold of the Manhattan Institute argues that New York's September 14 Board of Regents vote to end Regents exams as a graduation requirement repeats mistakes already visible in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania. In Massachusetts, after voters repealed the MCAS requirement, two-thirds of districts defined competency as a D-, and 10th-grade MCAS results have since fallen. In Pennsylvania's Philadelphia, the portion of students demonstrating readiness through state exams fell as the "evidence-based" pathway grew, with easy industry credentials such as a two-hour ladder-safety course doing much of the work. Arnold says New York's pilot schools already show signs of weaker rigor, including project assessments that test little core knowledge and invite AI misuse. She concludes that exit exams provide external motivation, keep teachers on track and make it harder to weaken expectations, so removing them relieves schools of responsibility for graduates' preparation.
points: Massachusetts shows that replacing an exit exam with local competency standards can drift to the lowest passing bar, with two-thirds of districts choosing a D-.
Pennsylvania's alternative pathways let districts raise graduation rates on paper by steering students to easy credentials, while most students still struggle with basic reading and math.
Portfolio and project assessments in New York's pilot put less emphasis on core knowledge and give students weeks to use AI between classes.
Educators in the pilot told reporters that alternatives would be easier than the Regents, which undercuts leaders' claims that expectations are not dropping.
An independent, transparent exam gives students a reason to care and gives schools an incentive to ensure real preparation.
quotes: Those states’ experiences show that weakening graduation requirements reduces accountability for schools. New York shouldn’t follow their lead. Replacing objective standards will introduce nebulous requirements that exist mainly to boost graduation rates rather than help students learn.

Districts resorted to defining competency as the lowest passing grade. Two-thirds of districts set the bar at D-, another 18 percent at D, and 15 percent didn’t specify at all what counted as passing.
In Philadelphia, teachers report that students at schools under pressure to boost graduation rates resort to options like a two-hour online ladder-safety course.
State leaders insist that they are not dumbing down expectations, but educators in the pilot program seem to believe that the alternative measures are less rigorous than the Regents exams.
Project-based assessments also put less emphasis on students’ core knowledge and create greater potential for AI misuse.
The Regents exams avoid these issues while offering other benefits. They give students external motivation to care about their academic outcomes. They keep teachers on track.

New York state education leaders say the move away from the Regents exams is about lowering the stakes for students. In reality, they are relieving schools of the mandate to ensure that students are adequately prepared for graduation.
